title: Chemical Analysis in the TEM: the Bentley Factor
content: This talk is dedicated to the late Jim Bentley in celebration of his contribution to chemical analysis using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (and sometimes using SEM). For many, Jim Bentley was the inspiration in the SHaRE program which ran for many years at ORNL; it was an outstanding model for collaborative research and influential for so many, with Jim Bentley co-authoring 28 papers, including 7 journal papers, with 9 of my students. Our collaborations emphasized the chemical analysis of oxides [1-4], although the exploration of secondary fluorescence correction formulae is applicable to any materials [5-7]. Some of the topics we explored, such as the analysis of grain boundary films, are not so important in a world composed of nanoparticles. However, the secondary fluorescence correction may still be relevant even when the TEM specimen is perfect. We begin by revisiting 2 collaborative projects. The first [1] was a study of grain boundaries (GBs) in alumina paying attention to whether a thin amorphous phase was present or not and if its presence could be determined by chemistry. The conclusion was that the researcher must be very suspicious because grooves that occur at the surface can mislead the observer. The figure shows two dark-field images formed using diffuse scattering: (a) edge-on GB in A1203, (b) the same region when tilted; the GB now shows two bright lines.
